newsitem.title: USA: New Mexico town pays immigrants for discrimination.
newsitem.headline: New Mexico town pays immigrants for discrimination.

text.p: A small New Mexico town agreed Thursday to pay more than $260,000 to 11 Mexican immigrant families for having discriminated against them by selectively enforcing a ban on mobile homes.
The town of Hatch was charged by the 11 farmworker families and the U.S. Justice Department with violating the federal Fair Housing Act.

The lawsuits alleged that an ordinance barring mobile homes was only enforced in the area of town primarily populated by Mexican farmworkers. Hatch lies about 40 miles northwest of Las Cruces on the banks of the Rio Grande and touts itself as "The Chile Capital of the World".

"We cannot allow a town to use their zoning authority to deny decent housing to a group of people because of their national origin," said Assistant U.S. Attorney General for Civil Rights Deval L. Patrick.

All of the farmworkers involved in the suit were legal residents of the United States. They won a temporary restraining order in 1994 to prevent the town from enforcing the zoning ordinance, and Hatch earlier this year amended its zoning map to ease restrictions on mobile homes.

The settlement agreement was filed in a U.S. District Court in Las Cruces Thursday. After legal bills are paid, each of the 11 families will receive about $16,000, about four times more than their average annual income.
